title: Λέων καὶ λύκος καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Lion, the Wolf and the Fox
part: The Lion, the Wolf and the Fox (Chambry 205)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 205. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων γηράσας ἐνόσει κατακεκλιμένος ἐν ἄντρῳ.
sentences.tr: Leōn gērasas enosei katakeklimenos en antrōi.
sentences.l: A lion, having grown old, was sick, lying down in a cave.
sentences.n: κατακεκλιμένος is a perfect participle of state: he had lain down and was still lying. The imperfect ἐνόσει holds the illness open while the visitors come and go.

sentences.t: Παρῆσαν δ’ ἐπισκεψόμενα τὸν βασιλέα, πλὴν ἀλώπεκος, τἄλλα τῶν ζῴων.
sentences.tr: Parēsan d’ episkepsomena ton basilea, plēn alōpekos, talla tōn zōiōn.
sentences.l: And the rest of the animals were there to look in on the king — all except the fox.
sentences.n: ἐπισκεψόμενα is a future participle of purpose, the regular way of saying what someone has come to do. τἄλλα is a crasis of τὰ ἄλλα, the two words run together with the mark over the α. The neuter plural subject takes a plural verb here, παρῆσαν, where the strict rule would give the singular; the fables are not consistent about this.

sentences.t: Ὁ τοίνυν λύκος λαβόμενος εὐκαιρίας κατηγόρει παρὰ τῷ λέοντι τῆς ἀλώπεκος, ἅτε δὴ παρ’ οὐδὲν τιθεμένης τὸν πάντων αὐτῶν κρατοῦντα, καὶ διὰ ταῦτα μηδ’ εἰς ἐπίσκεψιν ἀφιγμένης.
sentences.tr: Ho toinyn lykos labomenos eukairias katēgorei para tōi leonti tēs alōpekos, hate dē par’ ouden tithemenēs ton pantōn autōn kratounta, kai dia tauta mēd’ eis episkepsin aphigmenēs.
sentences.l: The wolf, then, laying hold of the opportunity, accused the fox before the lion, on the ground that she counted for nothing the one who ruled them all, and for that reason had not even come to visit him.
sentences.i: The wolf, then, seized his chance and accused the fox before the lion: she counted the ruler of them all as nothing, and for that reason had not so much as come to visit.
sentences.n: κατηγορέω takes the genitive of the person accused, τῆς ἀλώπεκος, and the two participles τιθεμένης and ἀφιγμένης agree with it. ἅτε δή with a participle states the ground as fact on the narrator's own authority — it is ὡς with a participle that marks a cause as merely alleged; here what is stated as ground is nonetheless the substance of the wolf's charge. παρ’ οὐδὲν τίθεσθαι is to set a thing beside nothing, to rate it at nothing.

sentences.t: Ἐν τοσούτῳ δὲ παρῆν καὶ ἡ ἀλώπηξ, καὶ τῶν τελευταίων ἠκροάσατο τοῦ λύκου ῥημάτων.
sentences.tr: En tosoutōi de parēn kai hē alōpēx, kai tōn teleutaiōn ēkroasato tou lykou rhēmatōn.
sentences.l: But in the meantime the fox too was there, and heard the last of the wolf's words.
sentences.n: ἀκροάομαι takes the genitive of what is listened to. τῶν τελευταίων … ῥημάτων is split wide apart with τοῦ λύκου set inside it — ordinary Greek word order, and worth noticing because the eye must hold the first word until the last arrives.

sentences.t: Ὁ μὲν οὖν λέων κατ’ αὐτῆς ἐβρυχᾶτο.
sentences.tr: Ho men oun leōn kat’ autēs ebrychato.
sentences.l: The lion, then, roared against her.
sentences.n: κατά with the genitive is hostile: the roar is aimed at her, as an accusation is.

sentences.t: Ἡ δ’ ἀπολογίας καιρὸν αἰτήσασα· « Καὶ τίς σε, ἔφη, τῶν συνελθόντων τοσοῦτον ὠφέλησεν ὅσον ἐγώ, πανταχόσε περινοστήσασα, καὶ θεραπείαν ὑπὲρ σοῦ παρ’ ἰατρῶν ζητήσασα καὶ μαθοῦσα ; »
sentences.tr: Hē d’ apologias kairon aitēsasa· « Kai tis se, ephē, tōn synelthontōn tosouton ōphelēsen hoson egō, pantachose perinostēsasa, kai therapeian hyper sou par’ iatrōn zētēsasa kai mathousa ; »
sentences.l: And she, having asked for a chance to speak in her defence: « And which of those who have gathered, » she said, « has helped you as much as I, who have roamed round in every direction and sought out a cure for you from doctors and learned it? »
sentences.i: She asked leave to defend herself: « And which of those who have come, » she said, « has done you as much good as I, who have travelled round in every direction and got a cure for you from the doctors and learned it? »
sentences.n: The fox is left without a finite verb of her own: the participle αἰτήσασα leads straight into the speech, and outside the quotation nothing governs her. τοσοῦτον … ὅσον is the correlative pair, 'so much … as'. ἀπολογία is the speech a defendant makes at his trial, and the courtroom colouring runs through the whole scene.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ λέοντος εὐθὺς τὴν θεραπείαν εἰπεῖν κελεύσαντος, ἐκείνη φησίν· « Εἰ λύκον ζῶντα ἐκδείρας τὴν αὐτοῦ δορὰν θερμὴν ἀμφιέσῃ. »
sentences.tr: Tou de leontos euthys tēn therapeian eipein keleusantos, ekeinē phēsin· « Ei lykon zōnta ekdeiras tēn autou doran thermēn amphiesēi. »
sentences.l: And the lion having at once bidden her tell the cure, she says: « If, having flayed a wolf alive, you put on his hide while it is warm. »
sentences.i: When the lion at once bade her name the cure, she says: « If you flay a wolf alive and wrap yourself in his hide while it is still warm. »
sentences.n: Genitive absolute again, and then a historic present, φησίν, which brings the scene up close at its worst moment. The prescription is a bare εἰ-clause with a future verb and no main clause at all: the 'then you will be well' is left for the lion to finish, and he finishes it on the wolf.

sentences.t: Καὶ τοῦ λύκου αὐτίκα νεκροῦ κειμένου, ἡ ἀλώπηξ γελῶσα εἶπεν οὕτως· « Οὐ χρὴ τὸν δεσπότην πρὸς δυσμένειαν παρακινεῖν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς εὐμένειαν. »
sentences.tr: Kai tou lykou autika nekrou keimenou, hē alōpēx gelōsa eipen houtōs· « Ou chrē ton despotēn pros dysmeneian parakinein, alla pros eumeneian. »
sentences.l: And the wolf lying there at once a corpse, the fox, laughing, spoke thus: « One must not stir the master toward ill will, but toward good will. »
sentences.n: νεκροῦ is a predicate inside the genitive absolute: not 'the dead wolf lying' but 'the wolf lying dead'. δυσμένεια and εὐμένεια are the same stem under opposite prefixes, ill-mindedness and good-mindedness, and the fox's last word is the pair of them set side by side.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ὁ καθ’ ἑτέρου μηχανώμενος καθ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὴν μηχανὴν περιτρέπει.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ho kath’ heterou mēchanōmenos kath’ heautou tēn mēchanēn peritrepei.
sentences.l: The fable shows that he who contrives against another turns the contrivance round upon himself.
sentences.n: The same κατά with the genitive that carried the lion's roar now carries both halves of the moral, first against another and then against oneself. μηχανώμενος and μηχανήν are one word twice over, the doing and the thing done.
